newsitem.title: USA: GM prepares Pontiac, Mich., plant for production. [CORRECTED 00:15 18/07]
newsitem.headline: GM prepares Pontiac, Mich., plant for production. [CORRECTED 00:15 18/07]

text.p: Skilled trades workers were back inside General Motors Corp.'s Pontiac East plant Thursday for the first time in nearly three months, preparing its strike-idled assembly lines to begin building trucks again.
About 5,850 members of United Auto Workers Local 594 were scheduled to vote Friday afternoon on a new local contract agreement reached with GM Wednesday night after marathon negotiations.

"If all goes well in terms of getting the contract ratified and the task of getting the plant prepared, we would hope to resume production on Monday," said GM spokesman Jeffrey Kuhlman (corrects name of spokesman).
The plant is one of three factories that produce GM's full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks, but it builds the highly popular extended-cab models.

Burnham Securities auto analyst David Healy estimated that the strike cost GM about $350 million in lost profits. On Wednesday, GM said strikes in Pontiac and Oklahoma City together reduced its second-quarter net income by $490 million, although the auto giant still managed to earn $2.1 billion during the period, up 11 percent over a year ago.
Details of the agreement, which ends GM's longest-ever local plant strike and one of the longest in auto industry history, were not disclosed.
But union officials said Thursday that GM agreed to hire as many as 500 workers at the Pontiac East plant and at nearby truck engineering and development facilities.

About half of the new jobs are expected to be added at the assembly plant, as part of the deal, which roughly follows the 6 percent staffing increases GM granted to end strikes at truck plants in Janesville, Wis., and Fort Wayne, Ind. in the past year.

About 4,100 UAW members work at the assembly plant. The workers walked off their jobs on April 22 over demands for more jobs to replace retiring workers and ease an increasing workload. Some said they were not able to take vacations because GM was not able to relieve them.

But the automaker had resisted the union's job demands as part of a long-running effort to shrink its hourly work force to more competitive levels through retirements and normal attrition. A new-generation full-size pickup truck that GM is preparing to launch next year is expected to require 30 percent fewer workers to build than the current model.
Analysts said the walkout probably has delayed production of prototypes of the new trucks by up to two months.
GM said Wednesday that the Pontiac pact meets the needs of the Pontiac employees and "allows GM to meet its pre-established competitive targets."
The strike was the industry's longest since 1950, when the UAW shut down Chrysler Corp. down for 101 days in a national walkout. The UAW waged a 110-day national strike against GM in 1945 and 1946.

The strike is one of several the UAW has waged against GM this year. The automaker faces two new UAW strike deadlines on Tuesday at a transmission plant in Warren, Mich., and at a lighting plant in Anderson, Ind. A walkout at either plant could disrupt production at a number of plants.
